title: Ribera del Duero
description: Powerful Tempranillo from a high, cold plateau along the Duero river.
L: Ribera del Duero follows the Duero river for about 115 km across Castilla y León, in north-central Spain. Vineyards sit on the Meseta, the high central plateau, at 750 to over 1,000 m, among the highest in Europe. Soils mix limestone, clay, sand and chalky marl. It has about 26,000 hectares of vines.

The climate is extreme continental: long, cold winters, short, hot summers and a huge day and night range, sometimes 20 degrees. Hot days ripen the grapes; cold nights keep acidity and colour. Frost is a constant danger, even in late spring or early autumn; 2017 lost over half the crop to frost.
Huge day and night swings, frost
Why does Ribera's Tempranillo keep its freshness?
Cold nights on the high plateau
Altitude gives cold nights that preserve acidity.

Vega Sicilia, founded in 1864, made Ribera's greatest wine, Único, for over a century before the region was known. Alejandro Fernández's Pesquera, praised by critics in the 1980s, made the region famous. The DO was created in 1982 with only a handful of wineries; today there are over 300. Dominio de Pingus, since 1995, is another icon.

Ribera's grape is Tempranillo, locally called Tinto Fino or Tinta del País. It has adapted to the extreme climate with thicker skins and smaller berries than in Rioja, giving darker, more concentrated wines with black fruit, liquorice and firm tannin. Reds must be at least 75% Tinto Fino; since 2019, rules allow 100% and blends with Cabernet, Merlot, Malbec, and white Albillo.
Tinto Fino: thicker skins, darker wines

Ribera uses Spain's ageing categories: Joven, Crianza, at least 24 months, 12 in oak; Reserva, 36 months, 12 in oak; Gran Reserva, 60 months, 24 in oak. Many wines use French oak and have a modern, powerful style. Since 2019, white wines from Albillo Mayor are also allowed as Ribera del Duero.
Ribera's rules are close to Rioja's, with local names.
Vega Sicilia's Único blends Tinto Fino with some Cabernet Sauvignon and ages for about ten years before release.
How does Ribera's Tinto Fino typically compare with Rioja's Tempranillo?
Thicker skins and extreme climate give power.

Labels show Ribera del Duero DO, the producer, vintage and ageing category, with a back-label seal. Roble, oak, is an unofficial term for young wines with a few months in barrel. Many top wines don't use the categories at all, relying on the producer's name.

Ribera's classic pairing is lechazo, roast suckling lamb, cooked in wood-fired clay ovens in Aranda de Duero. It also suits grilled steak, game, chorizo, Manchego and aged sheep's cheese. Serve at 16 to 18 degrees, decanted when young; good Ribera ages 10 to 20 years.
Which dish is Ribera del Duero's classic match?
Roast suckling lamb in wood ovens.
Aranda de Duero has a network of medieval underground cellars, many still used for ageing wine.
